classification_signals: data on long-term spatial microclimate perception were acquired through interviews and microclimate measurements on three Dutch squares. (abstract, p.1)

The two research questions were investigated with different methods. The first question on the spatial configurations functioning as cues was investigated through the analysis of cognitive maps based on user interviews. The second question was inquired through comparison of the spatial configurations (including the analysis of geometric properties) that were assigned certain micro-climate properties with measurement results and microclimate literature. (section 2, p.2)
The study was conducted on three Dutch squares (Spuiplein in Den Haag, Neckerspoel in Eindhoven and Grote Markt in Groningen). (section 2, p.2)
To answer the first research question... we used cognitive maps. (section 2.1, p.4)
To acquire comparison data for validation of people's long-term experiences microclimate measurements were conducted parallel with the interview series. (section 2.2, p.5)
title: Immersed in microclimatic space: Microclimate experience and perception of spatial configurations in Dutch squares

findings.consequent: Perceived as 'too windy'
findings.quote: In all three squares these places are considered to be too windy.

findings.consequent: Higher wind speeds (measured)
findings.quote: The measurement data also support for all three squares that these areas indeed show higher wind speeds than the areas considered comfortable in terms of wind (also see Table 2).

findings.consequent: People's microclimate perception (windy) matches real wind climate (higher wind speeds)
findings.quote: we conclude that user's assessments of the open square areas to be "windy" matched well and that people have developed a good comprehension of the wind climate in these types of places.

findings.consequent: Perceived as 'too windy'
findings.quote: Places perceived to be "too windy"... foot of a tall building

findings.consequent: Higher wind speeds (measured)
findings.quote: Here measurement data for two such places supported that these areas indeed had higher wind speeds than the areas considered comfortable in terms of wind (also see Table 2).

findings.consequent: Windy conditions due to downwash effects
findings.quote: Other research on wind patterns confirms that the areas around the feet of tall buildings are generally windy due to downwash effects (Bottema, 1993b; Littlefair et al., 2000).

findings.consequent: People's microclimate perception (windy) is justified by measurements and research
findings.quote: So we conclude that in this case the perception of people about these places being "windy" is justified, both by the measurement results and other research.

findings.consequent: Perceived as 'too windy'
findings.quote: Places perceived to be "too windy"... entrance of street canyon

findings.consequent: Higher wind speeds (measured)
findings.quote: The street entrance areas clearly show higher wind speeds in our measurements than areas that are perceived comfortable in terms of wind.

findings.consequent: Higher wind speeds due to wind funneling and venturi effects
findings.quote: Firstly street canyons can work as wind funnels increasing wind speeds due to higher pressure "venturi" effects (Bottema, 1999; Johnson and Hunter, 1999).

findings.consequent: More gusty winds due to corner pressure effects
findings.quote: Furthermore, angular building corners... are often more gusty due to corner pressure effects (see Fig. 22; Bottema, 1993a, 1999).

findings.consequent: People's microclimate perception (windy) correctly reads cues for wind climate
findings.quote: In this case people often correctly read the cues for wind climate in these types of spaces.

findings.consequent: Perceived as 'too windy'
findings.quote: Places perceived to be "too windy"... passage

findings.consequent: Higher wind speeds (measured)
findings.quote: Our measurements had only one point that is situated at the end of a passage-type of space, but the measurement results here were once more higher than the ones in the places considered comfortable in terms of wind.

findings.consequent: Acts as strong wind funnels
findings.quote: This configuration type's air flow physics show a clear tendency to act as strong wind funnels (Bottema, 1993a; Littlefair et al., 2000).

findings.consequent: People's microclimate perception (windy) is appropriate
findings.quote: Again, in this case people's interpretations are quite appropriate.

findings.consequent: Perceived as 'comfortable in terms of wind'
findings.quote: Places perceived to be "comfortable in terms of wind"... Semi-enclosed area

findings.consequent: Lower wind speeds (measured)
findings.quote: All the measurements taken in these areas showed indeed lower wind speeds than the ones taken in places considered to be "windy".

findings.antecedent: Semi-enclosed area (e.g., café terrace bounded by building and wind-screens)
findings.consequent: Offers wind protection from three sides
findings.quote: These areas can offer wind protection from three sides. For example, in case of the typical wind-screens of ~1.5 m height that usually flank the café terraces a wake area is approximately 10-15 m (Fig. 25; Oke, 1987; Robinette and Mc Clennon, 1983).

findings.consequent: People's microclimate perception (comfortable in wind) has a high probability to be suitable
findings.quote: So people's interpretation of this spatial cue "semi-enclosed area" has a high probability to be suitable.

findings.consequent: Perceived as 'comfortable in terms of wind'
findings.quote: Places perceived to be "comfortable in terms of wind"... foot of a low building

findings.consequent: Lower wind speeds (measured)
findings.quote: The averaged measurements taken in two typical spots also show lower wind speeds than the places perceived "windy".

findings.consequent: Provides wind protection for two directions (cavity/wake area)
findings.quote: Also the buildings provide wind protection for two directions as a part of the cavity area on the windward side or a wake area on the lee-side (also see Fig. 25; Oke, 1987; Robinette and Mc Clennon, 1983).

findings.consequent: People's assessment of wind comfort might be based more on reading spatial cues than actual wind microclimate
findings.quote: So we assume that people's assessment might be based more on the reading of the spatial cues than the wind microclimate.

findings.consequent: Perceived as 'comfortably sunny'
findings.quote: Places perceived to be "comfortably sunny"... Semi-enclosed areas

findings.consequent: People's perception of 'sunny' is only partly appropriate (62% match with shadow simulations)
findings.quote: The total match of 62% indicated that people's perceptions of sun tend to be only partly appropriate, with still a large percentage unexplained.

findings.consequent: People's perception of 'comfort in terms of sun' might be based more on the spatial setting than the real sun/shadow climate
findings.quote: It seems that in this case people's perception of "comfort in terms of sun" is based more on the spatial setting than the real sun/shadow climate.

findings.consequent: Perceived as 'comfortably sunny'
findings.quote: Places perceived to be "comfortably sunny"... foot of a low building

findings.consequent: People's perception of 'sunny' is rather appropriate (66% match with shadow simulations)
findings.quote: The total match of 66% shows that people's perceptions of sun tend to be rather appropriate, with still quite a large percentage unexplained.

findings.antecedent: Foot of lower buildings (with good sun-orientation, often café terraces/benches)
findings.consequent: Perception of 'comfortable in terms of sun' might be influenced by friendly atmosphere and unconscious choice to stay in sunny spots
findings.quote: In these places the perception of "comfortable in terms of sun" might also have to do with the fact that people enjoy a friendly atmosphere and relate this to their overall feeling of comfort. Or people unconsciously choose sunny places to stay and thus base their experience on the time they spend in these sunny spots.

findings.consequent: People's interpretation of spatial configurations and microclimate perception leads to developed schemata on microclimatic space
findings.quote: From this research we can conclude that there are significant correlations between people's interpretation of spatial configurations and microclimate perception and that people have developed schemata on microclimatic space.

findings.consequent: Function as spatial cues for microclimate
findings.quote: Concerning the first research question... we can answer with yes. There are spatial configuration types that are associated with certain microclimate properties and this was in general supported by measured microclimate data.

findings.consequent: People's acuity for general microclimate reality is good for most places, but exceptions exist (e.g., sun exposure)
findings.quote: many people have developed acuity for the general microclimate reality for most of the places. The cues seem to be a tool to "quick-scan" spaces on most probable microclimate properties. However, there are exceptions. Not in all cases the interpretation of the spatial configuration on their expected microclimate was right. Especially the data on sun-exposure showed this.

findings.consequent: People's interpretations of microclimate generally have a good relation to reality
findings.quote: Yet, generally speaking, people's interpretations of spatial/visual cues for microclimate, most of the time, have a good relation to reality and misinterpretations of cues are more exception than rule.

limitations: Our findings represent only a little fraction of the plethora of relations that are expected to exist between spatial and microclimate perceptions. (section 3, p.12)
It would be worthwhile, for instance, to conduct similar research as the one presented here in other places that have very different sizes or spatial setups. (section 3, p.12)

It would be interesting to study this in different climate zones because it is very likely that people develop different schemata and interpretations of spatial cues for microclimate depending on the regional climate. (section 3, p.12)
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical mixed-methods study investigated how people's long-term microclimate perceptions relate to urban spatial configurations in three Dutch squares, using cognitive maps from interviews and microclimate measurements. Findings revealed that specific spatial configurations (e.g., central open squares, foot of tall buildings, street canyon entrances, passages) were consistently perceived as 'too windy,' a perception largely supported by actual wind speed measurements and microclimate literature on wind flow patterns. Conversely, semi-enclosed areas and the foot of lower buildings were perceived as 'comfortable in terms of wind' and 'comfortably sunny,' with wind perceptions generally aligning with measurements, but sun perceptions showing more variability and potential influence from social factors or unconscious choice. The study concludes that people develop schemata linking spatial cues to microclimate, which are generally accurate but can have exceptions, suggesting that urban design should primarily address real microclimate issues while acknowledging perceptual influences. Limitations include the study's focus on a limited number of spatial types and climate zones, suggesting a need for broader research across diverse urban contexts and climates.

mechanism_chain.description: The physical configuration of an urban square, specifically its openness (low H/W ratio), directly influences wind speeds and turbulence, which in turn leads to the perception of the space as 'too windy'.
